cells.tense: Here, at the end of a finished thing, your read of it is steady and you can hand it over.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: When you and someone wrap something up together, tell them the feeling under your assessment — the real version, out loud, to their face, once.
cells.core:
You can see what a finished thing actually is and still be gentle handing it over. The true sentence arrives at the size it can be heard, and after you say it, people know where they stand instead of guessing. That's the gift, and its shape is plain: something comes together, gets seen for what it is, then gets let go of — and you're someone who can say whether it came out the way it should have.

That costs something. Seeing straight at the end of a thing means saying the thing, to a person, and staying while they take it. So when the two of you finish something, give them the feeling underneath the assessment instead of the tidy summary. What you say plainly stops living in your head, and what you hand over, they get to keep.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's finished, and you can say it plain.
cells.verb: reading what's actually there, and saying it at the size it can be heard
cells.place: the moment something has finished coming together and gets let go of

cells.tense: You will have the whole verdict worded and ready before the thing has finished being made.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Take the project you're pushing hardest toward done, do only its next ordinary step this week, then close the notebook for the day, unfinished.
cells.core:
Where you see clearly, the clear read outruns the work by days. The verdict, the correction, the better version — all worked out before the thing is done, and carried around like a load to hold until you can set it down. The read is accurate. It isn't the work's own pace.

What's underneath is that a finished thing might get seen wrong, so you get there first. For one project you're driving toward done, do the next ordinary step — the step that was already next — then shut the notebook for the day and leave the rest unfinished overnight. It'll still be legible in the morning. A fire doesn't stay lit by being fed all night; it stays lit on steadier feedings.

cells.tense: You are standing back from a finished thing, and a clear read of it has not arrived.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: Ask one person close to you how something felt for them, then stay with their answer for a few sentences — no correcting, no jumping to the point.
cells.core:
Where seeing straight matters here, little is coming into focus. Things finish around you and you aren't quite at the table for it — off to one side, holding back, so the read doesn't land and you don't trust the one that does. It isn't that the knack is gone. It's that it hasn't been let near anything warm.

Working harder at it won't bring it back. Someone else's feeling, held simply, will. So ask one person close to you how something felt on their side — and stay there. Don't correct it, don't skip forward, don't land the point. Let their answer be the thing you're looking at for a few breaths. The read returns through being near what's real, not through forcing it.

cells.tense: Already you are naming what a shared thing means, and you would say you were just going along with everyone.
cells.act: make a ritual of the shared thing
cells.ask: Take something you share with someone and mark it on purpose this month — the same small gesture each time — then tell them you chose it.
cells.core:
The one deciding how a shared thing gets talked about is you — what the ending gets called, which version gets kept, how the group retells it. That naming is happening right now, and if someone asked you to account for it you'd say the room decided and you agreed. The meaning is coming from your side. The name on it got filed somewhere else.

Begin smaller than an idea. Take something you share with another person — a weekly call, a dinner, a walk after finishing a project — and mark it deliberately: same small gesture, said out loud once, so it's clearly a person's choice. Then tell them you chose it. That's the whole ask. A thing you claim stops being background. You'll feel it the first time someone hands the practice back to you.

attempts.check: The one unsupported claim in my draft is that the person has actually been the calm, clear-eyed one in a room that needed it — the record only gives the capacity, not the history, so every cell has to describe what the capacity does in a moment they could recognise, not what they have lived. A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not the steady one, I'm the one who can't stop going over it' — so the Too Much and Too Little cells must be opposite failures of one act, over-managing the seeing versus not letting it arrive, and the asks must work even if my read of which way it bends is wrong. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line that flatters the steadiness; the asks are written so they teach something either way, and none of them needs a safe person, money, or free time.
